text.tspan: Fresh food is displayed at a market.
When we buy what we need, a little care can make the experience better. Planning and
thinking about other people both help.
First, a short shopping list helps us buy only what we can use. For example, we check the
kitchen before choosing fruit and vegetables. This is a small thing that makes the day easier.
Second, asking questions helps us compare choices fairly. For example, we ask how long the
bread will keep before deciding how much to buy. We do not need a perfect day to do this well.
We can buy what we need more easily when we prepare and notice other people. These
simple steps give us a useful place to start.
BUILD YOUR OWN · State a clear main idea; develop two different points with examples; bring them together in the
conclusion. Each body paragraph needs a distinct point and a concrete example. The conclusion should connect the
argument rather than introduce a new proposal.
Give a new learner two simple tips about how to buy what we need. Use four short paragraphs: introduction, two developed
points, and conclusion. (Model: One possible outline: say what you want to do; explain the first step; explain a different
second step; say why the two steps help.)
